transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick sanity check — audio OK?
[00:04] Liam: Yeah we can hear you. Thanks Samir. I'm Liam from EdgeVault infra.
[00:08] Samir: Cool. Nina's our SE, she'll drive the tech bits. Nina, do you want to intro?
[00:12] Nina: Yep hi all, Nina Gomez, Platform SE at Redwood. We'll go through the shipping model we recommend for truly air-gapped sites, how activation keys get generated and bound, and call out driver and kernel sig requirements.
[00:23] Priya: For context, EdgeVault has an on-prem private cluster behind an HSM and no internet egress. We need a process where we can receive media and get licensed without a tunnel out.
[00:33] Nina: Perfect. We'll run through two patterns: 1) sealed SSD or encrypted USB media with signed manifest, and 2) an offline activation token exchange using a customer-signed CSR that you post from a jump box. Both avoid outbound connections as long as you can bring the media into the air-gapped environment.
[00:48] Tomas: If we go with the signed manifest route, what are the guarantees? We need to be sure the binaries aren't tampered with.
[00:54] Nina: Two layers — artifacts signed by Redwood's release key (we provide public key for verification) and SHA256 checksums for each file. The manifest itself is signed and also contains expected kernel module checksums for the driver package so you can verify kernel modules before insmod.
[01:10] Samir: We'll also include a small verification script you can run that exits non-zero if signature or checksum mismatch.
[01:15] Priya: About licensing — does Redwood issue perpetual keys, node-bound keys, or floating?
[01:20] Nina: We support multiple modes, but for air-gapped customers we usually do node-bound entitlements. The activation key is a signed JWT-like blob that contains host identifier fields — GPU serials, hostname, and optionally a TPM endorsement key fingerprint. The blob is signed by Redwood's offline licensing signer and can be validated locally.
[01:38] Liam: Can we review the data we need to send? We don't want to expose more than necessary.
[01:42] Samir: Minimal — GPU serial numbers, hostnames, OS kernel version, and a salt (random nonce) you generate. If you prefer TPM binding, we take a TPM EK pubkey fingerprint so we can sign to the TPM. We don't keep the serials in plaintext in the activation token; the token is scoped and has an expiry and audit fields.
[02:00] Priya: How does rotation look? Suppose we replace a node mid-contract.
[02:05] Nina: We issue revocation manifests and can generate replacement keys for the new serials. For offline customers, that typically happens through an RMA process — send new serials, we generate a replacement token and send on physical media or presigned link for transfer via a jumpbox.
[02:20] Tomas: Regarding drivers — our infra team runs RHEL 8.8 with kernel 5.14. We have A10L and A100 cards. Which driver versions are supported?
[02:29] Nina: We validated on Nvidia drivers 525 and 535 for kernel 5.14 and 5.15; for CUDA runtime we recommend CUDA 12.1 for the latest quantized kernels. We'll send a matrix but quick note: 540+ has some firmware changes that impact nv_peer_mem on certain distros, so we prefer 535 for now on RHEL8.
[02:47] Samir: Also note that if you need signed kernel modules for secure-boot, the driver modules must be signed with the host key; our package includes an unsigned module plus a recommended sig process and a .ko.sig placeholder.
[02:58] Liam: Is kernel module signing required? We run secure boot in prod.
[03:01] Nina: If secure-boot is enforced, yes. We'll provide guidance: either enroll our vendor key into your MOK or sign modules locally with your key. We can support both workflows in the runbook.
[03:12] Priya: Good. On performance side — we care about latency p95 under 40ms for 64-token completions. What's realistic on A100 with your q8_0 runtime?
[03:21] Nina: So, depends on batching and KV warming. For single-request low-latency mode (no batching) you can expect ~30–45ms p95 for short contexts on an A100 with q8_0 and the optimized kernels. If you allow micro-batching (2–4 requests pooled for 5–10ms), you can reduce avg cost and improve throughput but might push tail latency slightly. Important piece: if the KV cache is cold and you're loading large context checkpoints on first request, that first request can spike since the KV warmup may involve disk-to-GPU transfers. We recommend a warmup step that we include in the installer to prefill KV for your most common prompts prior to traffic.
[04:02] Tomas: How large are KV artifacts? We plan to run long chat sessions so KV size could be big.
[04:07] Nina: KV size is proportional to sequence length x hidden states. Typical warmup checkpoints for 8k context models are a few GB per shard. We'll provide prebuilt warmup snapshots for canonical tasks; customers can also generate their own by running the warmup tool in the bundle. We advise storing warmups on NVMe local storage and copying to GPU device memory at boot as part of runtime startup to avoid the first-request penalty.
[04:30] Liam: And batching windows — how does Redwood choose batch size at runtime?
[04:34] Nina: The runtime uses an adaptive batching algorithm with a short batching window (configurable 5–15ms) and max batch size per model profile. For on-prem you can cap both to meet latency SLOs. We'll share recommended defaults: window 8ms, max batch 8 for latency-sensitive endpoints. For throughput jobs you can increase windows and max batch.
[04:53] Priya: Quantization — you mentioned q4_k and q8_0. Any caveats running q4_k in production on A10?
[05:00] Nina: q4_k gives better memory savings but may slightly reduce quality for some instruction-following tasks. On A10, q8_0 tends to be safer if you need strong fidelity; q4_k is great if memory footprint is the bottleneck. We'll include perf delta numbers in the matrix — e.g., q8_0 p95 latency ~ +10–15% vs FP16 in our runs but tokens/sec per GPU increases.
[05:20] Tomas: Do we need to recompile kernels or use special CUDA libs provided in the bundle?
[05:24] Nina: The bundle contains prebuilt CUDA-compatible runtime libs compiled against CUDA 12.1 and cuBLAS/cuDNN pinned versions. We avoid kernel recompiles; however, if your distro pkgset is older, you may need to install specific glibc compat libs. We'll call out minimal package list in the runbook.
[05:40] Liam: How will you deliver the artifact? We prefer physical media for initial rollout.
[05:44] Samir: We can ship encrypted SSDs with a sealed manifest. Process: we ship FedEx signed package, you verify manifest checksum and signature, then run the installer in an isolated jumpbox. For future patches we can provide a presigned S3 link that you can pull via a bastion jumpbox or continue receiving physical media.
[05:59] Priya: For activation via CSR flow — can we generate a CSR inside our air-gap and have you sign something?
[06:05] Nina: Yes — you generate a CSR with the node info (and optionally TPM EK), copy it onto the media, we sign and return an activation blob containing the license. That blob includes expiry, entitlements, and a signature you validate offline. It's similar to an offline CA model.
[06:18] Tomas: We need to audit key usage. Does the activation blob include an audit chain?
[06:22] Samir: It includes an audit ID and timestamp, and we provide a signed revocation list file for customers to distribute when required. We also keep an internal audit log that we can provide under NDA.
[06:33] Priya: KMS integration — we mandate our HSM handles key material and rotate monthly. Can Redwood support HSM-wrapped license keys?
[06:40] Nina: Yes. For activation, we can issue keys encrypted to your KMS public key. The on-node agent will unwrap with the HSM. We support common KMS wrappers; we'll capture the exact vendor and alg in the action item.
[06:52] Liam: Are there any gotchas with PCI-e firmware or NVidia ECC modes that affect runtime?
[06:57] Nina: ECC should be left in the vendor-recommended mode; turning on some ECC profilers can add latency for small operations. Also watch BIOS PCIe ASPM settings — aggressive power saving can spike latency. We'll include a BIOS checklist.
[07:12] Tomas: For the warmup automation, how long does it take to prefill KV for an 8k context across 4 shards?
[07:18] Nina: Roughly a few minutes — depends on NVMe speed. On benchmark NVMe we saw 2–4 minutes to copy and initialize KV into GPU memory per shard.
[07:26] Priya: On licensing, what if a host is decommissioned mid-contract? Any prorate rules?
[07:31] Samir: Contract terms aside, our tooling supports revocation and reallocation of entitlements; billing/proration handled by sales. From a technical view we revoke tokens and issue replacements for the new serials.
[07:41] Liam: For on-call and support SLAs, do you offer remote assistance for air-gapped installs?
[07:45] Nina: Yes, we provide phone and scheduled onsite support as an add-on. For air-gapped installs we usually recommend a short remote session via your jumpbox during initial activation or an on-site engineer for the first deploy.
[07:57] Samir: Quick recap and owners: Nina will share driver compatibility matrix and warmup tooling docs; I'll upload the signed bundle and the presigned link; Tomas will provide GPU serials and preferred install dates; Priya will send KMS vendor info.
[08:10] Priya: Sounds good. Also please include explicit instructions for signing modules under secure-boot, we need that for our security review.
[08:16] Nina: Will do — that will be in the runbook.
[08:19] Liam: Any outstanding blockers from Redwood side?
[08:22] Samir: Not blockers, just deliverables. We'll try to get the bundle out by 12/10.
[08:27] Tomas: Great, thanks all.
[08:30] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the presigned link and the runbook.
[08:34] End of recording.
